pos: n. pl. (the Marian Exiles, c. 800 English Protestants who fled abroad under Mary I, 1553–1558)
etymology: Latin Maria, whence Marian, of Queen Mary; Latin exilium, banishment.
biblical_def: The Marian Exiles were the English Protestants — some eight hundred, with their households — who left the realm after Mary I's accession in 1553 rather than conform or burn. They settled in congregations at Strasbourg, Frankfurt, Zurich, Basel, Emden, Wesel, Aarau and above all Geneva, where John Knox and Christopher Goodman served the English church. The exile was the making of English Protestantism. At Geneva, Whittingham, Gilby, Sampson and their fellows produced the Geneva Bible of 1560, the first English Bible with verse divisions, roman type and marginal notes, which was the household Bible of the English-speaking world for eighty years; the Genevan psalter and Calvin's liturgy and discipline were learned at first hand. At Frankfurt the troubles over the Prayer Book rehearsed, in miniature, the vestiarian and presbyterian disputes of the next forty years. When Mary died in 1558 the exiles came home and filled the Elizabethan bishoprics, deaneries and pulpits, bringing Geneva with them. “Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exile as banishment, or the person banished, and refugee as one who flies to a place of shelter.
webster_full: EX'ILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country; the person banished.
REFUGEE', n. One who flies to a shelter or place of safety; one who flees his country.
CONGREGA'TION, n. A collection or assembly of persons for religious worship.
scriptures: Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?
corruption_summary: The eight hundred who fled Mary and came home with Geneva in their baggage.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The exile is sometimes described as a flight of the prudent while the brave stayed and burned, a judgment the exiles themselves anticipated and answered. Some stayed by conviction and died; others went by the Lord's own permission, and the Geneva Bible that came back in their luggage did more for England over the next century than their ashes would have done.

The principle to recover is that scattering is one of God's ordinary methods of propagation: the persecuted church at Jerusalem “went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4), and the men of whom the world was not worthy “wandered in deserts, and in mountains” (Heb 11:38). A church without a continuing city (Heb 13:14) can carry its treasure in a cart.

Hebrew nekar (H5236) — a strange or foreign land; Psalm 137:4.

“they wandered in deserts, and in mountains” (Heb 11:38) — the price of the Geneva Bible.
“How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?” (Psa 137:4) — five years abroad.

pos: n. (Robert Ferrar, c. 1500–1555, Bishop of St David's, burned at Carmarthen under Mary I)
etymology: Old German Hrodberht, bright in fame; Ferrar, from Latin ferrarius, a smith.
biblical_def: Robert Ferrar was a Yorkshireman, an Augustinian canon who embraced the Reformation, prior of Nostell, chaplain to Cranmer, and in 1548 consecrated Bishop of St David's in Wales — the first bishop consecrated by the English ordinal alone, without the old Latin rite. He set about enforcing the Reformed order in a remote and largely Welsh-speaking diocese, which made him enemies among his own chapter; they brought a long list of charges against him, part doctrinal and part administrative, and he was imprisoned in 1551 under Edward VI while the suits dragged on. Mary's accession settled the case differently. He was tried for heresy before Bishop Henry Morgan, refused to recant the married state of the clergy or the doctrine of the supper, was degraded and burned in the market place at Carmarthen on 30 March 1555. He had told a friend that if he stirred in the fire they should not believe his doctrine, and he did not stir. “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a martyr as one who suffers death in defence of the Christian faith, and to degrade as to deprive of office or dignity.
webster_full: MAR'TYR, n. One who suffers death in defense of the Christian faith; one who is put to death for his religion.
DEGRA'DE, v.t. To reduce from a higher to a lower rank; to deprive of office or dignity.
OR'DINAL, n. A book containing the order of divine service; the form of ordination.
scriptures: Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
corruption_summary: The first bishop consecrated by the English ordinal, burned at Carmarthen in 1555.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Ferrar's case is worth keeping because it shows how administrative grievance and doctrinal persecution interlock. His own chapter had been suing him for years over visitation fees, Welsh preaching and the use of diocesan property; when the regime changed, the same men found a charge that carried the stake, and the long dossier gave the trial an air of legality.

The principle to recover is the fixed point in such a tangle. Fear is to be reserved: “fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul” (Mat 10:28). The overcoming is by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, by men who “loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11) — which is what a man proves by standing still in the fire.
roots_lines: Greek apokteino (G615) — to kill, put to death; Matthew 10:28.
usage: “be thou faithful unto death” (Rev 2:10) — Carmarthen, 30 March 1555.
“I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course” (2Ti 4:7) — seven years of suits and a stake.
“they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11) — he did not stir in the fire.

pos: n. (Richard Bayfield, d. 1531, Benedictine monk turned smuggler of Tyndale's books, burned at Smithfield)
etymology: Old German Ricohard, strong in rule; Bayfield, from the Norfolk place-name.
biblical_def: Richard Bayfield was chamberlain of the Benedictine abbey of Bury St Edmunds, converted by books lent him by Robert Barnes, and twice imprisoned by his own abbot before escaping to the Low Countries. There he became the most effective book-runner of the English Reformation: he made three voyages bringing in Tyndale's New Testament, Tyndale's Obedience and Practice of Prelates, Frith's and Joye's works and continental Reformed divinity, landing them at London, Colchester and Norwich and distributing them through the universities. Sir Thomas More, as chancellor, hunted him; he was taken in 1531, tried before Bishop Stokesley, condemned as a relapsed heretic, degraded with some brutality, and burned at Smithfield on 4 December 1531. His chief crime was moving printed Scripture across water. The bishops burned the books at Paul's Cross and the books came back. “Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah hath burned” (Jer 36:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to smuggle as to import or export secretly against law, and a heretic as one who holds and teaches opinions repugnant to the established faith.
webster_full: SMUG'GLE, v.t. To import or export secretly goods which are forbidden by law.
HER'ETIC, n. A person under any religion, who holds and teaches opinions repugnant to the established faith.
RELAPSED', pp. Having fallen back into a former state or practice.
scriptures: Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah hath burned.
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: The monk who ran Tyndale's Testaments into England, burned at Smithfield in 1531.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Bayfield is a useful corrective to a picture of the English Reformation as a thing decided by kings and parliaments. Before any statute, Scripture came into England in bales of cloth and barrels, carried by men who knew the penalty; the official Bibles of 1537 and 1539 were possible because the unofficial ones had already created readers.

The principle to recover is the futility of burning the word. Jehoiakim cut up and burned the roll, and God said, “Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words” (Jer 36:28); for “the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8). Smithfield did not alter that arithmetic by one copy.
roots_summary: Hebrew megillah (H4039), a roll, scroll; saraph (H8313), to burn; dabar (H1697), word.
roots_lines: Hebrew megillah (H4039) — a roll, written scroll; Jeremiah 36:28.
Hebrew saraph (H8313) — to burn, consume with fire; Jeremiah 36:28.
Greek kakoucheo (G2558) — to treat ill, torment; Hebrews 11:37.

“the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) — against Paul's Cross.
“being destitute, afflicted, tormented” (Heb 11:37) — Smithfield, December 1531.

pos: n. (William Whittingham, c. 1524–1579, chief translator of the Geneva Bible, Dean of Durham)
etymology: Old German Willahelm, resolute helmet; Whittingham, from the place-name, the white meadow.
biblical_def: William Whittingham was a fellow of All Souls, Oxford, who travelled in France, Germany and Italy, married a relative of Calvin's, and became the leading figure among the English exiles at Geneva, succeeding Knox as their minister. He was the principal translator of the Geneva Bible: his own English New Testament of 1557 was the first printed in roman type, with numbered verses and italics for supplied words, and it became the basis of the complete Geneva Bible of 1560, which he saw through the press with Gilby and Sampson. He also versified several psalms for the Anglo-Genevan psalter. Returning in 1560, he was made Dean of Durham in 1563 and spent sixteen years there, resisting the choral and ceremonial habits of the cathedral and nearly losing his deanery in 1578 on the ground that his Genevan ordination was invalid; he died before the case was decided. The conventions he fixed — verse numbers, roman type, italic supplements — are in every English Bible printed since, the Authorized Version included. “The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart” (Psa 19:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a verse as a short division of any composition, and italic as the slender inclined letter first used by Aldus.
webster_full: VERSE, n. A short division of any composition; a line of poetry; a stanza.
ITAL'IC, a. Relating to Italy; the Italic letters are the slender inclined letters.
DEAN, n. In England, an ecclesiastical dignitary in cathedral churches.
scriptures: Psa 19:8
The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
corruption_summary: The Geneva Bible's chief translator, who gave English Bibles verse numbers and italics.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Whittingham's innovations are so universal that nobody thinks of them as choices. Verse numbers make a text citable, searchable and memorisable; italics for supplied words are an act of honesty, telling the reader where the translator has added to make English of Hebrew. Both were designed for a lay reader working without a priest.

The principle to recover is that honest apparatus serves understanding, which is the translator's whole business: “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). The word spoken must be “easy to be understood” (1Co 14:9), and the reader must be able to see where the text ends and the translator begins, because “holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21) and their translators did not.

Greek eusemos (G2154) — easy to be understood; 1 Corinthians 14:9.
Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, carry, be moved; 2 Peter 1:21.

“gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — verse numbers and notes.
“holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21) — hence the italics.

pos: n. (Anthony Gilby, c. 1510–1585, Geneva Bible translator, vicar of Ashby-de-la-Zouch and patriarch of the Puritans)
etymology: Latin Antonius, a Roman family name; Gilby, from the Lincolnshire place-name.
biblical_def: Anthony Gilby was a Cambridge Hebraist, one of the Marian exiles at Frankfurt and Geneva, and one of the three or four men who actually produced the Geneva Bible of 1560; the Old Testament work, with its heavy dependence on the Hebrew and its pointed marginal notes, is largely his. Returning in 1560, he became vicar of Ashby-de-la-Zouch under the patronage of the Earl of Huntingdon and made that Leicestershire town a centre and refuge of the puritan party for a quarter of a century — a place where silenced preachers found a pulpit and young ministers were trained. He never accepted the vestments or the ceremonies, wrote sharply against them, translated Calvin and Beza into English, and was consulted in every stage of the vestiarian and presbyterian disputes without ever being broken by them. He was, in the judgment of his contemporaries, the most learned Hebraist among the first Elizabethan Puritans. His rule was always the same: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a margin as the border or edge, and a note as a remark or annotation on a passage.
webster_full: MAR'GIN, n. A border; the edge, brink or verge of anything; the edge of a page.
NOTE, n. A remark, annotation or commentary on a passage of a book.
HE'BRAIST, n. One versed in the Hebrew language.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
corruption_summary: The Geneva Bible's Hebraist, who made Ashby a refuge for the puritan party.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Geneva notes Gilby helped write are the most criticised feature of that Bible, and the criticism has some force: a marginal note carries the authority of the page it sits on, and a reader may receive an interpretation as though it were text. James I disliked them for a different reason, that some were pointed about kings.

The principle to recover is the one Gilby applied to notes as to everything else: every human word about Scripture is tested by Scripture (Isa 8:20). Notes are helps and may err; the text they annotate is “given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16). A reader taught that distinction is safer with notes than without them.
usage: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — his rule for notes and ceremonies alike.
“All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) — the text, not the margin.
“ask for the old paths, where is the good way” (Jer 6:16) — Ashby-de-la-Zouch.

pos: n. (Thomas Sampson, c. 1517–1589, Dean of Christ Church, deprived in the vestiarian controversy)
etymology: Aramaic Te'oma, a twin; Hebrew Shimshon, Samson, of the sun.
biblical_def: Thomas Sampson was one of the Marian exiles, a translator of the Geneva Bible, and on his return Dean of Christ Church, Oxford. He declined the bishopric of Norwich rather than wear the prescribed vestments, and in 1565, with Laurence Humphrey of Magdalen, he refused the surplice and the square cap when Archbishop Parker enforced the Advertisements. Humphrey submitted; Sampson did not, and was deprived of his deanery — the first notable casualty of the vestiarian controversy, the dispute that gave the Puritan party its name and its character. He spent his later years as master of Wigston's Hospital in Leicester, preaching and writing, partly paralysed for his last fifteen years, still consulted and still unyielding. His case raised precisely the question the next century would fight over: whether a thing indifferent in itself can be commanded on pain of deprivation, and whether a minister may wear a garment he judges to be a relic of a false worship. “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vestment as a garment, particularly a long garment worn in religious ceremonies; and a surplice as a white garment worn by clergymen over their other dress.
webster_full: VEST'MENT, n. A garment; some part of clothing or dress, particularly a long garment worn in ceremonies.
SUR'PLICE, n. A white garment worn by clergymen of the established church over their other dress.
DEPRI'VE, v.t. To divest of an ecclesiastical preferment or dignity.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Rom 14:5
One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak.
corruption_summary: Christ Church's dean, deprived in 1565 for refusing the surplice and cap.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The vestiarian controversy looks trivial to modern eyes, and both sides knew the garments were in themselves indifferent. That was the whole difficulty. Sampson's argument was that a thing indifferent ceases to be indifferent when it is imposed as necessary and when its association in the people's minds is with a worship the realm had renounced.

The principle to recover is the care Scripture takes over such cases. “Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” (Rom 14:5) protects the conscience of the man who complies and of the man who refuses; and liberty is limited by its effect on the weak, lest it “become a stumblingblock to them that are weak” (1Co 8:9). What neither side may do is make an indifferent thing a test of office.

pos: n. (the Great Bible, 1539, the first English Bible authorised to be set up in every parish church)
etymology: So called from the size of its pages; Greek biblia, books.
biblical_def: The Great Bible of 1539 was the first English Bible appointed by royal authority to be set up in every parish church in the realm, where it was chained to a desk so that any parishioner could read it. It was prepared by Miles Coverdale at Thomas Cromwell's direction, revising Matthew's Bible against the Latin and the Hebrew and dropping the controversial notes; printing began in Paris and was finished in London after the French authorities seized the sheets. Cranmer wrote the preface to the second edition of 1540, from which it is sometimes called Cranmer's Bible. Its lasting legacy is not its text, which was superseded, but its Psalter: the version in the Book of Common Prayer, still sung in English cathedrals, is Coverdale's from the Great Bible rather than the Authorized Version's. Within three years the reading of it was restricted again by statute to the upper classes. For those three years an English labourer could walk into his parish church and read the Scriptures. “So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to authorise as to give authority or legal power, and a lectern by its root, to read, the desk from which lessons are read.
webster_full: AU'THORIZE, v.t. To give authority to; to empower; to make legal.
PAR'ISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the congregation.
CHA'IN, v.t. To fasten, bind or connect with a chain; to fasten in a secure manner.
scriptures: So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: The 1539 Bible chained in every parish church, and the Prayer Book Psalter.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The chained Bible is often cited as a symbol of the church withholding Scripture, which reverses the fact. The chain was there because the book was expensive and the desk was public: it was fastened so that it could not be stolen and therefore could not be taken away from the parish, like a reference book in a reading room.

The principle to recover is the purpose such an arrangement served: “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17), which requires the word to be within reach of the hearer. And the restriction imposed within three years is the standing reminder that an authorised Bible is a mercy that depends on no authority: “the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).

pos: n. (the Bishops' Bible, 1568, the official Elizabethan version and the base text of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Old English biscop, from Greek episkopos, an overseer; Greek biblia, books.
biblical_def: The Bishops' Bible was produced under Archbishop Matthew Parker and published in 1568, revised in 1572, as the Church of England's answer to the Geneva Bible. Parker parcelled out the books among about fifteen revisers, most of them bishops, each working on the Great Bible text with little coordination, and the result is uneven: some books carefully revised against the Hebrew and Greek, others barely touched, with a style that never caught the ear. It was appointed to be used in churches and went through some twenty editions, but it never displaced the Geneva Bible in the home, because the Geneva was cheaper, better translated and furnished with notes. Its real importance came later. When James I commissioned a new version in 1604, the rule given to the translators was that the Bishops' Bible was to be followed and as little altered as the truth of the original would permit; so the Authorized Version is formally a revision of it. “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) is a standard the committee of 1568 met unevenly and that of 1611 met magnificently.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a revision as a review for correction, and a bishop as an overseer or spiritual superintendent.
webster_full: REVI'SION, n. The act of reviewing; review; re-examination for correction.
BISH'OP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent or ruler.
EDI'TION, n. The publication of any book; an impression; the whole number of copies published at once.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Psa 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
corruption_summary: The 1568 official version, uneven in itself, and the base text the 1611 translators revised.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Bishops' Bible is the standing argument against the notion that an authorised version can be imposed. It had the archbishop, the bishops, the Convocation and the royal injunctions behind it, and English families went on buying the Geneva Bible for two generations because it was better. A translation lives by its quality and not by its licence.

The principle to recover is that translation is workmanship, to be judged as such: “a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15). The words of the LORD are themselves “as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psa 12:6), and God's word does not return void (Isa 55:11) — which is why 1611 could build so well on so uneven a foundation.
roots_summary: Greek orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight; spoudazo (G4704), to be diligent; Hebrew tsaraph (H6884), to refine.
roots_lines: Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, handle rightly; 2 Timothy 2:15.
Greek spoudazo (G4704) — to give diligence, study; 2 Timothy 2:15.
Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — to refine, try as metal; Psalm 12:6.
usage: “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) — met unevenly in 1568.
“as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psa 12:6) — and again in 1611.
“it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — twenty editions, and a better successor.

pos: n. (Michael Wigglesworth, 1631–1705, minister and physician of Malden, author of The Day of Doom)
etymology: Hebrew Mikael, who is like God; Wigglesworth, from the Yorkshire place-name.
biblical_def: Michael Wigglesworth was brought from Yorkshire to New England as a child, graduated at Harvard, and served the church at Malden in Massachusetts for nearly fifty years, practising medicine alongside the ministry because his health was too poor for preaching alone. In 1662 he published The Day of Doom, a poem of two hundred and twenty-four stanzas in ballad metre on the last judgment, which became the best-selling book of colonial America: one copy for every twenty persons in New England, learned by heart by children, and reprinted for a century and a half. It is a plain versification of the doctrine of judgment, written to be memorised rather than admired, and its most discussed passage is the plea of those who died in infancy. He also wrote God's Controversy with New-England, a jeremiad on the colony's declension. His verse has been mocked for two centuries by critics who missed its purpose, which was catechetical: to put before an ordinary family the scene Scripture describes. “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2Co 5:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines doom as judicial sentence, condemnation, and judgment as the act of judging, the final trial of the human race.
webster_full: DOOM, n. Sentence; judicial judgment; judicial sentence; condemnation.
JUDG'MENT, n. The act of judging; the act of the mind by which it compares ideas; the final trial of the human race.
BAL'LAD, n. A short narrative poem; a popular song.
scriptures: For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.

And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.
Heb 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil.
corruption_summary: Malden's minister-physician, whose Day of Doom was colonial America's best-seller.
corruption_paragraphs: The Day of Doom is the stock exhibit whenever Puritan New England is to be presented as a culture of terror, with Wigglesworth as the man who frightened children for a living. The poem repays actual reading. It is a versified catechism on a doctrine the New Testament states repeatedly, written by a sick country pastor for families who could not afford a library, and its tone toward the fearful is gentler than its reputation.

The principle to recover is that the judgment is a fact to be taught and not a mood to be managed: “it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27); “God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing” (Ecc 12:14). A generation taught nothing about it is not thereby comforted, only unprepared.

pos: n. (Samuel Sewall, 1652–1730, Massachusetts judge, the only witch-trial judge to repent publicly, author of the first American antislavery tract)
etymology: Hebrew Shemuel, heard of God; Sewall, from Old English Sigeweald, victory-ruler.
biblical_def: Samuel Sewall was a Massachusetts merchant, magistrate and at last Chief Justice of the colony, and he sat in 1692 as one of the judges of the Salem witchcraft court, which condemned nineteen people to death on evidence that would not have hanged a dog. Alone among the judges, he came to see what he had done. In January 1697, on a public fast day, he stood in the Old South Church while his minister read out his confession, taking what he called the blame and shame of it and asking the pardon of God and man; and he kept that day as a private fast for the rest of his life. In 1700 he published The Selling of Joseph, the first antislavery tract printed in America, arguing from Scripture that Africans are sons of Adam and co-heirs with the English, and that man-stealing is a capital crime under the law of God. He also wrote on behalf of the Indians and against the harsh treatment of them. His diary, kept for fifty-six years, is the fullest record of life in early New England. “whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Pro 28:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to confess as to own, acknowledge or avow a crime or fault, and manstealing as the act of stealing a human being.
webster_full: CONFESS', v.t. To own, acknowledge or avow, as a crime, a fault, a charge.
MAN'STEALER, n. One who steals and sells men; a kidnapper.
RETRAC'TION, n. The act of withdrawing something advanced; recantation.
scriptures: He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.

He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
Psa 32:5
I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah.
corruption_summary: The Salem judge who publicly repented, and the first American to print against slavery.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Sewall is nevertheless used in both directions by people who have not read him. He is cited as proof that the Puritans were murderous, and cited as proof that they could repent, and he is actually evidence of something more useful: that a man formed by the catechism had somewhere to go when he discovered he had helped kill the innocent, and knew what to do when he got there.

The principle to recover is the mechanism of that recovery. “He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Pro 28:13) was a sentence he had known since childhood, and it cost him his reputation to obey it. From the same Scriptures he learned that man-stealing is a capital crime (Exo 21:16) and that the requirement is “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8).
